title: Apologeticum
author: Tertullian
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0275.stoa009.perseus-lat2, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit the Perseus Digital Library and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: De sanguinis pabulo et eiusmodi tragicis ferculis legite, necubi relatum sit (est apud Herodotum, opinor), defusum brachiis sanguinem ex alterutro degustatum nationes quasdam foederi conparasse. Nescio quid et sub Catilina degustatum est. Aiunt et apud quosdam gentiles Scytharum defunctum quemque a suis comedi.
passages.english: Concerning the feeding on blood and such tragic dishes, read where it is related (it is in Herodotus, I think) that certain nations, having poured blood from their arms and tasted it from each other, made [it the pledge of] a treaty. Something was also tasted under Catiline. They say too that among certain tribes of the Scythians each dead man is eaten by his own people.
passages.notes: "necubi" is odd here (normally "lest anywhere"); it is taken in the sense "[see] whether somewhere"/"where". "foederi conparasse" is rendered loosely as "made [it the pledge of] a treaty".

passages.original: Sed nec operae locum video. Totum enim hoc mundi corpus sive innatum et infectum secundum Pythagoram, sive natum factumve secundum Platonem, semel utique in ista constructione dispositum et instructum et ordinatum cum omni rationis gubernaculo inventum est. Imperfectum non potuit esse quod perfecit omnia.
passages.english: But I do not see room for [such] work either. For this whole body of the world, whether unborn and unmade according to Pythagoras, or born and made according to Plato, was certainly found, once [and for all], in this construction of it, arranged and furnished and ordered with every governance of reason. That which perfected all things could not have been imperfect.

passages.original: Est et ille de lyricis (Pindarum dico) qui Aescolapium canit avaritiae merito, quia medicinam nocenter exercebat, fulmine iudicatum. Malus Iuppiter, si fulmen illius est, impius in nepotem, invidus in artificem. Haec neque vera prodi neque falsa confingi apud religiosissimos oportebat.
passages.english: There is also that one among the lyric poets (I mean Pindar) who sings that Aesculapius was condemned by the thunderbolt as he deserved for his greed, because he practised medicine harmfully. Jupiter is wicked, if the thunderbolt is his: impious toward his grandson, envious toward a craftsman. Such things ought neither to be published if true nor invented if false among the most religious [of peoples].

passages.original: Nunc ut constaret illos deos esse, nonne conceditis de aestimatione communi aliquem esse sublimiorem et potentiorem, velut principem mundi perfectae potentiae et maiestatis? Nam et sic plerique disponunt divinitatem, ut imperium summae dominationis esse penes unum, officia eius penes multos velint, ut Plato Iovem magnum in caelo comitatum exercitu describit deorum pariter et daemonum.
passages.english: Now, granting that it were established that they are gods, do you not concede, by common estimation, that there is someone more exalted and more powerful, a sort of ruler of the world, of perfect power and majesty? For most people too arrange the divine in such a way that they would have the command of supreme dominion rest with one, and its duties with many, as Plato describes great Jupiter in heaven accompanied by an army of gods and *daimones* [spirits] alike.

passages.original: Memorat et Plato maiorem Asiae vel Africae terram Atlantico mari ereptam. Sed et mare Corinthium terrae motus ebibit, et vis undarum Lucaniam abscisam in Siciliae nomen relegavit. Haec utique non sine iniuria incolentium accidere potuerunt.
passages.english: Plato also records that a land larger than Asia or Africa was snatched away by the Atlantic sea. And an earthquake drank up the Corinthian sea, and the force of the waves cut off Lucania and relegated it to the name of Sicily. These things certainly could not have happened without harm to the inhabitants.

passages.original: Ubi vero tunc, non dicam deorum vestrorum contemptores Christiani, sed ipsi dei vestri, cum totum orbem cataclysmus abolevit, vel, ut Plato putavit, campestre solummodo?
passages.english: But where then were, I will not say the Christians, despisers of your gods, but your gods themselves, when the flood wiped out the whole world, or, as Plato thought, only the lowlands?

passages.original: Socratis vox est: Si daemonium permittat. Idem et cum aliquid de veritate sapiebat deos negans, Aesculapio tamen gallinaceum prosecari iam in fine iubebat, credo ob honorem patris eius, quia Socratem Apollo sapientissimum omnium cecinit.
passages.english: It is Socrates' saying: "If the *daemonium* [divine spirit] permits." The same man, too, even when he had some taste of the truth in denying the gods, nevertheless at the very end ordered a cock to be sacrificed to Aesculapius, out of honour, I suppose, for his father, because Apollo had proclaimed Socrates the wisest of all men.
passages.notes: "prosecari" literally means to have the sacrificial portions cut off, that is, to sacrifice. "His father" refers to Apollo as the father of Aesculapius.

passages.original: Age iam, si qui philosophus adfirmet, ut ait Laberius de sententia Pythagorae, hominem fieri ex mulo, colubram ex muliere, et in eam opinionem omnia argumenta eloquii virtute distorserit, nonne consensum movebit et fidem infiget etiam ab animalibus abstinendi propterea?
passages.english: Come now, if some philosopher should assert, as Laberius says following the opinion of Pythagoras, that a man comes from a mule, a snake from a woman, and should twist every argument toward that opinion by the power of his eloquence, will he not win assent and fix belief, even to the point of abstaining from animals on that account?

passages.original: Multi apud vos ad tolerantiam doloris et mortis hortantur ut Cicero in Tusculanis, ut Seneca in Fortuitis, ut Diogenes, ut Pyrrhon, ut Callinicus. Nec tamen tantos inveniunt verba discipulos quantos Christiani factis docendo.
passages.english: Many among you urge the endurance of pain and death, as Cicero in the Tusculans, as Seneca in his Chance Events, as Diogenes, as Pyrrho, as Callinicus. Yet their words do not find as many disciples as the Christians [find] by teaching through deeds.
passages.notes: Seneca's "De fortuitis" is a lost work. Callinicus is not securely identified.
